The Blue-black Grosbeak Cyanoloxia cyanoides is a Neotropical passerine common in lowland forest understory. Eggs of this species are notable for their size; from measurements of egg length at 23.5 millimeters and width at 17.3 millimeters, we calculated an initial wet mass of 3.68 grams [Ww0 = 3.68 grams] using the formula for a prolate spheroid. Hatchlings emerge after an incubation period of 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days], a duration consistently recorded in nests where average ambient temperature was monitored at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] in the nest environment. Females then typically achieve an ultimate adult body mass of 33.6 grams [Wwi = 33.6 grams], while males, exhibiting the reverse sexual size dimorphism common in this genus, attain a slightly lower maximum adult mass of 30.6 grams [Wwi = 30.6 grams]. These masses are representative of medium-sized cardinals, and the modest 3.68 gram hatchling weight represents only about eleven percent of adult female mass, a proportion typical of altricial songbirds.

Developmental milestones in the nest follow a rapid schedule when thermal conditions are warm. Under typical active-season temperatures of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], young grosbeaks fledge the nest at 11.5 days after hatching [tx = 11.5 days after hatching], an early departure that likely reduces predation risk despite the nestlings still being relatively undeveloped. This fledging event occurs well before the full attainment of adult body mass. Data from growth curves of captive-reared individuals indicate that the onset of sexual maturity, or puberty, occurs at approximately 33 days after hatching [tp = approximately 33 days after hatching] when maintained at this same elevated temp at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]erature regime. This remarkably short period to maturation is considerably faster than in many other cardinalids of similar adult size, suggesting a life-history strategy prioritizing early reproductive potential in a short-lived, high-mortality environment.

Reproductive output in the Blue-black Grosbeak is modest but consistent across the breeding season. Field studies indicate that females typically produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and, under favorable conditions in the core of the range, may attempt a single clutch in a given year [F_R_i = single clutch in a given year]. This translates to a maximum annual reproductive rate of two eggs per year, a value that appears to be an adaptive ceiling given the high energetic demands of biparental provisioning in a seasonally resource-limited understory habitat. The first successful breeding attempt in this species occurs at an age of 1.1 years since birth [tR = 1.1 years since birth], as measured in wild populations where the average environmental temperature during the breeding season was 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This first reproduction is delayed relative to the attainment of puberty, likely because young birds require additional time to establish a territory, secure a mate, and accumulate sufficient body condition to initiate a nesting attempt.

Metabolic rates in Cyanoloxia cyanoides have been investigated under controlled laboratory conditions. Maximum basal metabolic rate (BMR) for an active adult individual was measured at 67.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 67.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the respirometry chamber was held at a stable 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. A slightly higher maximal value of 69.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 69.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour] was recorded from a separate individual under the same ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], indicating minor intraspecific variation in aerobic capacity. These oxygen consumption rates are relatively high for a passerine of this adult body mass, possibly reflecting the energetic costs of a high-protein diet of insects and berries and the maintenance of a large home range in dense forest. Such physiological data are critical for understanding the energy budget constraints that shape the species' life-history parameters.

Longevity records for the Blue-black Grosbeak in the wild are scarce, but the maximum recorded lifespan based on banding returns is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] for individuals experiencing the thermal conditions typical of their range at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan is relatively short compared to some larger Neotropical passerines, aligning with the species' rapid developmental rate and early age at first breeding. The life-history strategy thus appears to be one of rapid maturation, high early investment in reproduction, and a comparatively short total lifespan. The combination of a 33-day period to puberty (33 days after hatching) [tp = 33 days after hatching] and a 10-year maximum lifespan (10 years) [am = 10 years] places this species at the faster end of the slow-fast continuum for New World seedeaters and grosbeaks, a pace likely driven by high adult predation pressure and the necessity of exploiting ephemeral food resources in its lowland forest habitat at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
